title: Jnaneshwar
hook: four children turned away, and a buffalo that recites the Veda

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nayanars one last time: Sambandar, milk on his lips, pointing at the sky and singing his answer to who fed you. When a sharp question came, what did you point to? Day nine hundred thirteen.

Four children walk into a town of learned Brahmins with a request. They are brothers and a little sister, and they've been shut out by their community their whole lives, through no fault of their own. They want to be accepted. The scholars look them over and start to laugh. One of them points at a buffalo plodding by, and makes a joke about names. Today the path moves north and west, into the Marathi-speaking country, and meets the second of those children: Jnaneshwar.
screen: `FOUR CHILDREN, SHUT OUT.` → `THE SCHOLARS LAUGH.` → `A BUFFALO WALKS BY.`

segments.voice: Here is the story as tradition tells it. The children's father had left home to become a sannyasi, a renunciant. His teacher then sent him back to his wife and household life. To their community, a monk who goes home has broken the order of things, and the family is cast out. Four children are born into that: Nivritti, Jnanadev, Sopan, and their sister Muktabai. Before long, the story says, they are on their own. So they go to the Brahmins of Paithan to ask for a letter of purification that would let them belong. The scholars aren't moved. When they hear the second boy's name, Jnanadev, which carries the Sanskrit word for knowledge, someone mocks him: names mean nothing, look, that buffalo has a name too. Jnaneshwar doesn't argue. The story says he answers that the same Self lives in the buffalo as in him, and places his hand on its head. And the buffalo begins to recite the Veda, the sacred text these men have spent their lives learning. Another telling adds that when someone whips the buffalo, the marks rise on the boy's back. The scholars fall silent, and some tellings say they then grant the letter. Notice what the boy does not do. He doesn't prove that he deserves to belong. In the story, he shows that the line they drew, between people worth hearing and creatures that don't count, was never real. And the voice comes from the lowest place in the scene, an animal in the street. Over the next two days we'll see him keep doing it: carrying the highest teaching to whoever happens to be standing there.
screen: `A MONK WHO WENT HOME.` · `THE BRAHMINS OF PAITHAN.` · `THE SAME SELF IN THE BUFFALO.` · `THE VEDA FROM AN ANIMAL'S MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath come and go. Bring to mind a creature you usually don't think about much: a pigeon on a ledge, a dog on your street, an insect on the window. Let it be there in your mind, breathing too, alive in its own way. Then bring to mind a person you tend to look past. Hold them both for a while, with no conclusions. If you pray, you can hold them before God, in words you already use. The bell holds the time.
Jnaneshwar. Also called Jnanadev. The Marathi poet-saint who, the story says, made a buffalo recite the Veda to answer the people who shut his family out.
Your line: Jnaneshwar. Today, listen properly to one voice you usually treat as background. Day nine hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Jnaneshwar is honored across Maharashtra, especially by the Varkari tradition; his shrine is at Alandi, and stories of his childhood, including the buffalo at Paithan, are told and staged by devotees.
